meaning: next time; on the next occasion

senses.en: next time: the next occasion something happens

examples.en: Next time it's on me.
examples.analysis: 下次 is a time word at the front, before the subject; 我下次请你 is just as natural. 请你 here means 'treat you' (I pay), so this is what you say when a friend has just paid for the meal.

examples.en: Don't forget next time!
examples.analysis: A request about the future: 下次 + 别 'don't' + verb. 别忘了 is the everyday set phrase for 'don't forget'.

examples.en: When are you coming again?
examples.analysis: 下次 follows the subject 你 and comes before 什么时候 'when' and the verb 来. Like other time words, it goes before the verb, not after it as 'next time' does in English ('come next time').

related.en: measure word for occurrences: 一次 'once'
next, before a time unit: 下个星期 'next week'

meaning: class (group of students); work shift; measure word for scheduled runs

senses.en: class: a group of students who study together (我们班 'our class')
for scheduled runs of buses, trains and flights (最后一班车 'the last bus')
work shift, as in 上班 'go to work' and 夜班 'night shift'

examples.en: There are thirty students in our class.
examples.analysis: 班 is a noun here: 我们班 'our class', with no 的, as in 我们学校 'our school'. 有 + number + 个 + noun says how many the group contains: 三十个学生 'thirty students'.

examples.en: What time does the last bus leave?
examples.analysis: Here 班 is a measure word: 一 + 班 + 车 counts one scheduled run, so 最后一班车 is 'the last bus (of the day)'. 几点 'what time' comes before the verb, and 开 means 'to leave' for a vehicle.

examples.en: He's not in our class.
examples.analysis: 我们班的 = 'someone from our class': 的 at the end turns 我们班 into 'a person belonging to our class', so no noun is needed after it. 不是 negates the whole thing: 'he isn't one of ours'.

collocations.en: shuttle bus (for a company or school)

related.en: class, lesson: the teaching, not the group of students

senses.en: a class or lesson: one session of teaching (今天有课 'I have class today')
a course or subject (汉语课 'Chinese class')
a lesson in a textbook (第一课 'Lesson 1')

measure.note: 两节课 'two class periods'; 门 mén for a course: 一门课

examples.en: I don't have class tomorrow. What about you?
examples.analysis: 没课 'have no class' is 没有课 with 有 dropped, which is common in speech. 课 is a plain noun here, the thing you have or don't have. 你呢 asks the listener the same thing: 'what about you?'

examples.en: Is Chinese class hard?
examples.analysis: 汉语课 'Chinese class': the subject name sits right before 课, with no 的. 难不难 asks yes-or-no by saying the adjective, then 不, then the adjective again. This form does not take 吗: say 难不难？ or 难吗？, not both.

examples.en: Where is today's class held?
examples.analysis: 课 is moved to the front as the topic, and its verb 上 ('attend, hold', as in 上课) comes last, after 在哪儿 'where'. Literally: 'today's class, where do we have it?'

collocations.en: to have class; to teach a class

related.en: class: the group of students, not the lesson

meaning: to go to work; to be at work; to start work

senses.en: to go to work; to work at a regular job (他在医院上班 'he works at a hospital')
to start the working day (几点上班 'what time do you start')

examples.en: What time do you start work?
examples.analysis: 上班 here is 'start work'. 几点 'what time' comes before the verb, where Chinese normally puts time expressions. Answer in the same frame: 我九点上班 'I start at nine'.

examples.en: I'm not working today.
examples.analysis: 不 + 上班 states a plan or fact about today: 'I'm off today'. 不 is for not going (today, or as a habit); for 'didn't go to work' in the past, people say 没上班.

examples.en: Where does he work?
examples.analysis: 在哪儿上班 is the everyday way to ask where someone works. As with other activities, 在 + place goes before the verb, not after it as in English: 他在医院上班 'he works at a hospital'.

collocations.en: office workers; people with a regular nine-to-five job

senses.en: mountain; hill (山 covers both; 小山 is a small hill)

examples.en: The mountains here are so high!
examples.analysis: 这儿的山 'the mountains here': the place comes first and 的 links it to 山. Chinese nouns have no plural ending, so 山 can be one mountain or many. 真 + adjective makes an exclamation: 'so high!'

examples.en: Is it cold up on the mountain?
examples.analysis: 山上 'on the mountain': noun + 上 makes a place, as in 楼上 'upstairs'. The place opens the sentence, then 冷不冷 asks 'cold or not?'.

examples.en: There's a mountain right behind my house.
examples.analysis: Place + 是 + thing says what is at a place: 'behind my house is a mountain'. 就 stresses how close it is, 'right there'. 我家 'my home' takes no 的.

collocations.en: to climb a mountain; to go hiking

senses.en: clean, free of dirt (干净的衣服 'clean clothes')
after a verb, 'clean' as the result: 洗干净 'wash clean'

examples.en: Your room is so clean!
examples.analysis: 干净 is the predicate on its own, with no 是: Chinese adjectives work like verbs. 真 'really, so' makes it an exclamation; about someone's room it is a compliment, the kind you say when you visit their home.

examples.en: Is the cup clean?
examples.analysis: A yes/no question: noun + adjective + 吗, again with no 是. Answer 干净 'it's clean' or 不干净 'it's not clean'.

examples.en: The clothes didn't come out clean.
examples.analysis: 干净 comes after the verb 洗 as its result: 洗干净 = 'wash until clean'. 没 negates the result: the washing was done, but the clothes did not end up clean. 衣服 is the topic at the front.

senses.en: tree

examples.en: What kind of tree is this?
examples.analysis: 什么 + noun asks 'what kind of…': 什么树 'what tree, what kind of tree'. The question word stays where the answer goes: 这是苹果树 'it's an apple tree'.

examples.zh: 我们去树下边坐一下儿吧。
examples.en: Let's go sit under the tree for a bit.
examples.analysis: 树下边 'under the tree': noun + 下边 'below' makes a place, here the place you go to. 一下儿 after 坐 means 'for a little while', and 吧 makes it a suggestion.

examples.en: There are a lot of trees outside my house.
examples.analysis: Place + 有 + thing says what is somewhere: 'at my door there are many trees'. 很多 'a lot of' goes straight before the noun, usually without 的.

meaning: to eat; to have a meal

senses.en: to eat; to have a meal (any meal, not only rice)
to go out for a meal with someone (一起吃饭 'eat together'); in 请你吃饭 the 'treat' comes from 请

examples.en: Come on, let's go eat!
examples.analysis: 走 here means 'let's go', said to get people moving. 吃饭 + 去 puts the purpose before 去, a common spoken order; 去吃饭 means the same.

examples.en: Where do you have lunch?
examples.analysis: 中午 + 吃饭 is a common way to say 'have lunch': the time word tells you which meal. Order: subject, time, 在 + place, then the verb.

examples.en: I haven't eaten yet.
examples.analysis: 还没 + verb + 呢 = 'not yet': 还 'still' + 没 'haven't', and 呢 marks that the situation is still the case. A natural answer to 你吃饭了吗?

collocations.en: to treat someone to a meal

senses.en: next to, beside: X旁边 'next to X'
on its own: 'nearby, at the side' (旁边有… 'nearby there is…')

examples.en: There's a shop next to my place.
examples.analysis: Place + 有 + thing: 我家旁边 'next to my home' sets the location, then 有 introduces what is there. 有个 is 有一个 with 一 dropped, very common in speech.

examples.en: Why don't you sit next to me?
examples.analysis: 旁边 follows its reference point: 我旁边 'next to me', literally 'my side'. It goes straight after 坐 as the place where you sit. 吧 makes the invitation friendly.

examples.zh: 车站旁边有吃饭的地方吗？
examples.en: Is there anywhere to eat next to the station?
examples.analysis: The statement frame X旁边有… plus 吗 for a yes/no question. 吃饭的地方 'a place to eat': 吃饭 + 的 describes 地方 'place'.

collocations.en: the person next to you; people nearby

senses.en: eight (8)

examples.en: I start work at eight.
examples.analysis: 八点 'eight o'clock' is number + 点. The time goes before the verb 上班, not at the end as in English. Without a word like 明天 'tomorrow', it usually describes a routine.

examples.en: I live on the eighth floor.
examples.analysis: Number + 楼 names a floor: 八楼 'the eighth floor', with no word for '-th'. 住 + place without 在 is common in speech; 我住在八楼 means the same.

examples.en: Are you free on the 8th?
examples.analysis: Number + 号 gives a day of the month: 八号 'the 8th'. 有时间 'have time' is a common way to ask whether someone is free (有空 is equally common); the date comes before it.

meaning: ten cents: one tenth of a yuan (spoken)

senses.en: money unit, one tenth of a yuan (10 fen); the spoken word for 角 jiǎo

examples.en: The milk is three fifty.
examples.analysis: Prices stack from big to small: 三块 'three yuan' + 五毛 'five tenths' = 3.50. No verb is needed between the item and its price. In speech the last unit is often dropped: 三块五.

examples.en: You're still fifty cents short.
examples.analysis: A cashier's line. 差 'to be short of' + amount: 差五毛 'fifty cents short', with 还 'still'. 毛 is often followed by 钱 'money' in speech; 还差五毛 means the same.

examples.en: Are the buns eighty cents each?
examples.analysis: Item + 一个 + price gives a price per piece: 包子一个八毛 'buns, eighty cents each'. 八毛 = 0.80 yuan. 吗 turns the statement into a check.

related.en: fen, one hundredth of a yuan

senses.en: often, frequently; goes before the verb (= 常常)

examples.en: I often go there to eat.
examples.analysis: 常 sits before the verb phrase it describes: 常 + 去那儿吃饭 'often go there to eat'. 去 + place + 吃饭 is the purpose pattern: go somewhere to do something.

examples.en: Do you come here often?
examples.analysis: Adverb + verb, then 吗 for a yes/no question. Answer 常来 'yes, often' or 不常来 'not often'. 来 'come' because the speaker is here.

examples.en: He isn't home much.
examples.analysis: 不常 'not often' puts 不 right before 常; 不常常 is uncommon. 在家 'be at home' is the verb phrase being described.

senses.en: China; before a noun, 'Chinese' (中国菜 'Chinese food')

examples.en: Have you ever been to China?
examples.analysis: 去过 + place = 'have been to': 过 after the verb marks something you have experienced at some point. 中国 is the object, then 吗 makes it a yes/no question.

examples.en: I really like Chinese food.
examples.analysis: 中国 + noun, with no 的, means 'Chinese …': 中国菜 'Chinese food'. 很 before 喜欢 adds degree: 'really like'.

examples.zh: 她不是中国人，是日本人。
examples.en: She's not Chinese, she's Japanese.
examples.analysis: Country + 人 gives nationality: 中国人 'a Chinese person'. 不是 X，是 Y corrects a guess, 'not X but Y', with the subject left out of the second half.

related.en: Chinese (the language, spoken or written): 说中文 'speak Chinese'

senses.en: seven (7)

examples.en: I get up at seven.
examples.analysis: 七点 'seven o'clock' comes before the verb 起床 'get up'. Without a word like 明天 'tomorrow', the sentence usually describes a routine; in context it can also be a plan.

examples.en: There are seven of us.
examples.analysis: Number + 个 + 人 counts people. With no verb, 我们七个人 is what you tell a waiter: 'we're a party of seven'. 我们有七个人 means the same.

examples.en: Are you coming to Beijing in July?
examples.analysis: Number + 月 names a month: 七月 'July', the seventh month. The month goes before the verb 来, and 吗 asks yes or no.

senses.en: a dish; the food served at a meal (做菜 'to cook')
vegetables; greens
a cuisine (中国菜 'Chinese food')

measure.note: 一个菜 'one dish' (casual); 道 dào is the standard counter for a dish served as a course: 这道菜 'this dish'; 盘 pán for a plateful

examples.en: Your cooking is delicious!
examples.analysis: 你做的 'that you make' describes 菜: the clause + 的 comes before the noun. 菜 here is the cooked food. 真好吃 'really tasty' is a typical compliment to a host.

examples.en: What kind of food do you feel like?
examples.analysis: 什么菜 'what dishes, what kind of food': 菜 is what you choose from a menu. 想 + verb = 'feel like doing'.

examples.en: Eat more vegetables and less meat.
examples.analysis: Set against 肉 'meat', 菜 means 'vegetables'. 多 and 少 go before the verb to mean 'more' and 'less': 多吃 'eat more', 少吃 'eat less'. The kind of advice a doctor or parent gives.

meaning: yuan, the unit of Chinese money (written or formal; casual speech says 块)

senses.en: yuan, the basic unit of Chinese money; used in writing, on price tags and in announcements

examples.en: Admission is fifty yuan.
examples.analysis: Item + price with no verb, the style of a sign or a ticket-office announcement. 元 is the official unit; a friend telling you the price would more likely say 五十块.

examples.en: Two thousand yuan? That's way too expensive!
examples.analysis: Repeating a price you have just read off a sign or screen, as a question; said aloud, most people would say 两千块？. 两 is the usual form before 千: 两千 'two thousand'. 太 + adjective + 了 = 'too…'.

examples.zh: 车票多少钱？一百二十元。
examples.en: How much is the ticket? 120 yuan.
examples.analysis: 多少钱 asks a price; a clerk reading from a screen or sign answers number + 元. Aloud, most people say 一百二十块. 一百二十 is 'a hundred and twenty': Chinese says the 一 before 百, and needs no 'and'.

meaning: grandma (father's mother); a polite way to address an old woman

senses.en: grandmother on the father's side
a friendly, polite way for children and younger people to address an elderly woman who is not a relative

measure.note: 一位奶奶 (polite); 个 in casual speech

examples.en: My grandma is eighty this year.
examples.analysis: 我奶奶 'my grandma': with close family, 的 is usually dropped (我的奶奶 is also correct). Age is number + 岁 with no verb; 了 at the end marks that she has now reached that age.

examples.en: Have a seat here, ma'am.
examples.analysis: 奶奶 used to address an elderly stranger, for example when you give up your seat on a bus. 您 is the polite 'you', and 吧 makes the offer gentle.

examples.en: Do you often go to see your grandma?
examples.analysis: 看 + person = 'visit': 去看奶奶 'go see Grandma'. Chinese leaves out 'your' when it is clear who is meant. 常 before the verb phrase means 'often'.

related.en: grandma on the mother's side (standard term; 姥姥 is the northern colloquial one; both above HSK 2)

senses.en: last year

examples.en: I went to Beijing last year.
examples.analysis: 去年 is a time word before the verb. 去 appears twice: in 去年 it means 'gone by' (the year that has passed), and the verb 去 means 'go'. 了 marks the trip as done.

examples.en: Where were you working last year?
examples.analysis: Chinese verbs don't change for tense: 去年 alone puts the question in the past. Order: subject, time, 在 + place, verb.

examples.en: I didn't go home last year.
examples.analysis: 没 negates something that did not happen: 'didn't go home'. 去年 tells you when. Said about a whole year, 回家 usually suggests going back to your family's home or hometown.

collocations.en: since last year; starting last year

senses.en: to drive a car or other vehicle (开 'operate' + 车 'vehicle')

examples.en: Can you drive?
examples.analysis: 会 + verb = 'know how to', for a learned skill: 会开车 'can drive'. 吗 makes it a yes/no question; answer 会 'yes' or 不会 'no'.

examples.en: Let me give you a ride.
examples.analysis: Two verb phrases in a row: 开车 (how) + 送你 'take you (there)'. 吧 makes it an offer: 'let me give you a ride'.

examples.en: Don't look at your phone while you're driving!
examples.analysis: 开车 at the front sets the situation, 'when driving', with no word for 'when' needed. 别 + verb is 'don't'.

senses.en: wind

examples.en: It's very windy today.
examples.analysis: Chinese describes wind by size: 风大 'the wind is big' = 'windy'. 今天 is the topic, 风 the subject and 很大 the description, with no 是.

examples.en: Is it windy outside?
examples.analysis: The same 风 + 大 frame as a yes/no question, with the place 外边 'outside' first. Without 很 it is a plain 'is it windy?'; 风很大吗 would ask 'is it very windy?'.

examples.en: It's too windy. Don't go out.
examples.analysis: 太…了 'too…' gives the reason, and the second half follows from it. The 了 after 别出去 signals a change of plan: 'don't go out after all'.
